paper.title: A Bussgang-based Latent Lifting Method: Discrete RIS Channel Estimation and Beamforming
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of discrete phase-shift optimization in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided multiuser communication systems. Practical RIS hardware often utilizes low-resolution phase shifters, leading to challenging combinatorial optimization problems. To address this challenge, we propose a Bussgang-based latent lifting (BuLL) method that represents discrete phase shifts as quantized outputs of continuous latent variables. Our BuLL method calibrates the Bussgang gain and distortion covariance under a reference distribution and keeps these moments fixed during deterministic latent optimization. These fixed moments are then used to construct a distortion-aware continuous surrogate that incorporates reference-averaged discretization effects without penalty terms. For uplink channel estimation, we develop a matrix quadratic transform-based algorithm to optimize a mean-square-error surrogate. For downlink beamforming, we develop a generalized power iteration-based RIS phase-shift optimization algorithm for a spectral efficiency (SE) surrogate. Numerical results demonstrate improvements in channel estimation accuracy and sum SE over conventional benchmarks in the evaluated low-resolution RIS settings.

paper.title: Intelligent Reflecting Surface for ISAC: From Beamforming to Joint Design With Surface Orientation
paper.abstract: Rotatable semi-passive intelligent reflecting surfaces (SIRSs) provide an additional spatial degree of freedom (DoF) by proactively adjusting the orientation, while dedicated sensors directly receive target echoes. To exploit this DoF for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), we investigate the joint optimization of SIRS rotation, base station (BS) transmit beamforming, and SIRS phase-shifts to minimize the Cramér-Rao bound (CRB) for target's spatial-frequency estimation subject to per-user communication signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) constraints. We first establish an orientation-dependent system model that characterizes the effective aperture gains, based on which the CRB is derived. To gain useful insights, closed-form expressions of the beamforming and rotation designs are derived in the sensing-only and communication-only cases. For the co-located user and target case, we further characterize the condition under which the sensing-oriented rotation design also satisfies the communication requirement. In the single-user single-target case with ideal unit aperture gains, we analyze the channel correlation and its impact on ISAC performance. For the general multi-user case, an effective method based on the genetic algorithm is developed. Numerical results demonstrate the superiorities of the rotatable SIRS over the fixed-orientation SIRS and show that jointly optimizing the SIRS orientation and beamforming can improve the effective aperture gains and the correlation between communication and sensing channels.

paper.title: Towards in vivo photon dosimetry using radiation-sensitive mixed-core ultrasound phase-change contrast agents
paper.abstract: Objective. Advanced radiotherapy applies complex treatment plans that require verification of the beam delivery. Therefore, in vivo dosimetry, measuring delivered radiation doses directly on the patient, has become increasingly important. Radiation-sensitive phase-change nanodroplets were recently proposed for in vivo radiation sensing. The radiation-induced conversion of superheated nanodroplets into microbubbles generates ultrasound contrast from which radiation deposition can be derived. While successful for in vivo proton range verification, previously used nanodroplet formulations were not suitable for in vivo photon dosimetry due to stringent requirements on the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core. Here, we used a mixed-core strategy, combining different perfluorocarbons in the same nanodroplet core, to modulate the photon response and droplet stability at body temperature. Approach. Lipid-shelled nanodroplets with different cores (pure octafluoropropane, pure decafluorobutane and a 17:4 (v/v) octafluoropropane:decafluorobutane mixture) were dispersed in deionized water in phantom containers and irradiated with a photons at various temperatures. Simultaneous high-frame rate ultrasound acquisition allowed to link ultrasound contrast generation to the radiation delivery. Nanodroplets were characterized using 19F NMR spectroscopy. Main results. Photons induced nanodroplet-mediated ultrasound contrast strong enough for clinical applications at body temperature. A clear trade-off was observed between a stronger photon response and maintaining sufficient droplet stability. Neither octafluoropropane (lacking stability) nor decafluorobutane (lacking photon response) cores proved suitable. On the contrary, the mixed-core formulation exhibited a strong photon response with minimal background already at small radiation doses (0.1 Gy). This paves the way for future in vivo dosimetry.

## **Towards in vivo photon dosimetry using radiation-sensitive mixed-core ultrasound phase-change contrast agents** Bram Carlier[1,2] , Reza Bahrami Gorji[2] , Qingyuan Tan[3] , Meritxell Gambús-Marfà[1,4] , Uwe Himmelreich[1] , Meng-Xing Tang[3] , Koen Van Den Abeele[2] , Sophie V. Heymans[2,5] 1Department of Imaging & Pathology, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium 2Department of Physics, KU Leuven, Kortrijk, Belgium 3Department of Bioengineering, Imperial College London, United Kingdom 4Institut Químic de Sarrià (IQS), Universitat Ramon Llull (URL), 08017, Barcelona, Spain 5Department of Cardiovascular Sciences, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium ## **0. Abstract** _Objective._ Advanced radiotherapy treatments apply complex treatment plans that require careful verification of the beam delivery. Therefore, in vivo dosimetry, measuring delivered radiation doses directly on the patient, has become increasingly important. Radiation-sensitive phase-change nanodroplets were recently proposed for in vivo radiation sensing. The radiation-induced conversion of superheated nanodroplets into echogenic microbubbles generates ultrasound contrast from which radiation deposition can be derived. While successful for in vivo proton range verification, previously used nanodroplet formulations were not suitable for in vivo photon dosimetry due to stringent requirements on the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core. Here, we used a mixed-core strategy, combining different perfluorocarbons in the same nanodroplet core, to modulate the photon response and droplet stability at body temperature. _Approach._ Lipid-shelled nanodroplets with different cores (pure octafluoropropane, pure decafluorobutane and a 17:4 (v/v) octafluoropropane:decafluorobutane mixture) were dispersed in deionized water in phantom containers and irradiated with a preclinical photon irradiator at various temperatures. Simultaneous high-frame rate ultrasound acquisition allowed to link ultrasound contrast generation to the radiation delivery. Nanodroplet yield and composition were determined using[19] F NMR spectroscopy. _Main results._ For the first time, photons induced nanodroplet-mediated ultrasound contrast strong enough for clinical applications at body temperature. A clear trade-off was observed between a stronger photon response (increased degree of superheat) and maintaining sufficient droplet stability. Neither octafluoropropane (lacking stability) nor decafluorobutane (lacking photon response) cores proved suitable. On the contrary, the mixed-core formulation exhibited a strong photon response with minimal background already at small radiation doses (0.1 Gy). Future work will optimize the nanodroplet synthesis to improve reproducibility in view of quantitative dosimetric read-outs. _Significance._ We demonstrated the feasibility to modulate the photon radiation response of superheated nanodroplets at body temperature using a mixed-core formulation. This yielded radiation-induced ultrasound contrast sufficiently strong for future in vivo dosimetry. ## **1. Introduction** Radiotherapy is one of the cornerstones of cancer therapy, able to benefit about half of the cancer patients (Lievens _et al_ 2020). Technological advances facilitate highly conform treatment delivery, but the associated steep dose gradients make treatments prone to uncertainties. These arise from the image-based treatment planning process, patient motion, setup errors or anatomical changes throughout the treatment, and can result in underdosage of the tumor or excessive healthy tissue exposure if not properly accounted for (Mijnheer _et al_ 2013). In vivo dosimetry (IVD) measures the received radiation dose directly on or inside the patient (Mijnheer _et al_ 2013), ensuring correct dose delivery to the tumor target, preventing erroneous healthy tissue exposure and contributing to quality assurance protocols (Chow and Ruda 2025). As a result, IVD has become increasingly important in the radiotherapy workflow, with a plethora of dosimetry solutions available. One-dimensional dosimeters including thermoluminescent detectors (TLDs), optically-stimulated luminescent detectors (OSLDs), plastic scintillating detectors (PSDs), diodes, and metal oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) have a strong clinical track record, but are essentially point based measurement devices and thus not suitable to capture complex 3D dose distributions (Olaciregui-Ruiz _et al_ 2020). While the use of such detectors in array configurations solves part of the problem, the accurate evaluation of sharp dose gradients still relies strongly on the detector positioning, which is typically of low spatial resolution and limited to the patient’s surface. Film dosimeters provide highly resolved 2D dose information, but require intensive processing (radiographic) or strict read-out protocols (radiochromic) (Bjegovic _et al_ 2025, Olaciregui-Ruiz _et al_ 2020, Mijnheer _et al_ 2013). Moreover, they are made for single use and positioning is mostly limited to the surface of the patient. Electronic Portal Imaging Devices (EPIDs) use flat panel detectors integrated in the treatment device to monitor the transit dose. The dose delivery inside the patient is determined through the use of patient CT data and back projection algorithms (Mijnheer 2017). While relatively easy to integrate in current radiotherapy workflows, with several commercial solutions available (Kadoya _et al_ 2018, Olaciregui-Ruiz _et al_ 2020), some limitations remain. For example, the quality of the dose information depends on the adequacy of the used CT scans and the lack of tissueequivalence of the detector requires careful calibration to perform absolute dosimetry (Nelms _et al_ 2010). In addition, EPID dosimetry is restricted to applications where a clear transit dose is present, making it unsuitable for hadron therapy or internal radiotherapy (Bjegovic _et al_ 2025). Cherenkov imaging can be used to verify dose delivery by capturing the visual photons released when charged particles move faster through tissue than the speed of light (Darafsheh _et al_ 2024). Given the limited penetration depth of visual light, Cherenkov imaging is however limited to superficial applications such as skin and breast irradiation. Finally, radiacoustic imaging utilizes ultrasound waves generated during the thermoelastic expansions of tissues upon pulsed dose delivery to capture true 3D dose distributions directly in the patient (Sun _et al_ 2023, Bjegovic _et al_ 2025). While particularly promising for FLASH radiotherapy, where high radiation doses are delivered in short pulses, the technique is still in its infancy with many challenges remaining, e.g. poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), limited view artifacts, and the complex influence of tissue heterogeneity and acoustic attenuation on the quantitative relationship between the detected ultrasound signals and the radiation dose (Bjegovic _et al_ 2025). To overcome the limitations of currently available in vivo dosimetry solutions, we developed radiation-sensitive phase changing ultrasound contrast agents. In particular, superheated nanodroplets can convert into echogenic microbubbles upon irradiation, thereby generating strong ultrasound contrast from which the dose delivery can be assessed (Carlier _et al_ 2020, Heymans _et al_ 2021). Nanodroplets can be sensitized to different types of ionizing radiation by varying the degree of superheat of their liquid core as described by the theory of radiation-induced nucleation of superheated emulsions (D’Errico 2001, Heymans _et al_ 2021). The reduced degree of superheat (𝑠, equation 1) is a key parameter to characterize the radiation sensitivity: **==> picture [257 x 27] intentionally omitted <==** with Tb and Tc referring to the boiling and critical temperature of the superheated liquid, and T the operation temperature. With increasing degree of superheat, less energy is required to trigger droplet vaporization, hence ionizing radiation with lower linear energy transfer (LET) can initiate droplet vaporization. Specifically, protons can induce ultrasound contrast from s ≈ 0.42, while electrons released during photon therapy require at least s ≈ 0.51 (D’Errico 2001), as their peak LET is lower. Above the sensitization limit, the radiation response increases exponentially, until s ≈ 0.65, beyond which the liquid becomes so unstable that spontaneous vaporization occurs. Note that these values were determined for naked microemulsions, while the nanodroplets used in our previous and current studies are additionally encapsulated by a polymeric or lipidic shell. We confirmed the potential of radiation-sensitive nanodroplets for in vivo proton range verification using nanodroplets with a perfluorobutane core and a poly(vinyl alcohol) shell (Carlier _et al_ 2024a, Collado-Lara _et al_ 2022). However, for photon radiotherapy, the low LET of electrons required excessive heating of the perfluorobutane core (to ~65 °C) before a photon response was observed, preventing in vivo applications (Carlier _et al_ 2024b). To achieve the same degree of superheat and thus radiation response at body temperature, a nanodroplet core of lower boiling point is needed. At the same time, it is important that the nanodroplets do not become too unstable to handle. In the context of acoustic droplet vaporization (ADV) of phase-change contrast agents, where droplet vaporization is triggered by high-pressure ultrasound waves instead of ionizing radiation, a similar trade-off was observed in terms of droplet stability and acoustic pressures required to trigger phase change. This was resolved by combining multiple perfluorocarbon liquids in the same nanodroplet core, allowing to tune the required vaporization pressure by changing the ratio of the core liquids (Matsunaga _et al_ 2012, Riemer _et al_ 2023). Here, we utilized this mixed-core approach for the first time to tune the nanodroplet radiation sensitivity to photons at body temperature (37 °C). First, we illustrate the influence of the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core on the photon response and demonstrate the inadequacy of pure perfluorocarbon cores. On the contrary, a 17:4 (v/v) OFP:DFB mixed-core combines a good stability at body temperature with a strong radiation response. For this formulation, we evaluated the reproducibility of the photon response under different irradiation conditions and linked our observations back to the nanodroplet synthesis. Finally, we explored the necessary next steps towards quantitative dosimetry. ## **2. Materials & Methods** ## **2.1. Nanodroplet preparation via the microbubble condensation method** Radiation-sensitive nanodroplets were prepared from microbubble precursors as described previously (Zhang _et al_ 2019, Matsunaga _et al_ 2012). Briefly, a lipid mixture was prepared by dissolving 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC) and 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3phosphoethanolamine-N-[amino(polyethylene glycol)-2000] (DSPE-PEG-2000) in a 9:1 molar ratio. The solvent used was a 16:3:1 (v/v) solution of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), propylene glycol, and glycerol. Lipids were purchased from Avanti Polar Lipids, Inc. (Alabaster, AL, USA), and solvents were obtained from Merck (Hoeilaart, Belgium). A volume of 1 mL of the resulting solution with 1 mg/mL total lipid concentration was transferred to a 2 mL glass vial and sealed hermetically. Afterwards, 21 mL of perfluorocarbon gas was injected in the headspace (~17 mL with relief needle and the final ~4 mL after removal of the relief needle to allow pressure build-up). The perfluorocarbon gas was either pure OFP, pure DFB or a 17:4 (v/v) mixture OFP:DFB. After injection, the glass vial was mechanically agitated for 3 x 30 s in a bubble shaker (Capmix, 3M ESPE Deutschland Gmbh, Seefeld, Germany). This microbubble precursor solution was consequently submerged in an ice-salt bath (~ -5 °C) for 5-10 minutes. Then, the solution was transferred to a 1 mL Luer Lock syringe, subsequently sealed with a closed stopcock valve and eventually manually pressurized until the opaque bubble solution turned transparent, indicating successful microbubble condensation. Droplets were stored on ice and used immediately (<30 minutes) after preparation. ## **2.2. Nanodroplet / microbubble characterization** The nanodroplet yield and core composition were determined by quantifying the perfluorocarbon content using[19] F NMR spectroscopy (400 MHz Avance II NMR spectrometer, Bruker Biospin GmbH, Rheinstetten, Germany). We added an internal standard of known concentration (200 µL of 20 mM fluorocytosine) to the 5 mm NMR tube containing 100 µL of nanodroplets and 100 µL deuterated water. We used a free induction decay size of 65536 data points, and acquired a spectral width of 249 ppm with a transmitter frequency of 376.49 MHz. Signals were averaged 880 times, yielding an acquisition time of 20 minutes. To quantify the NMR spectra, peaks were integrated after phase and baseline correction using Topspin Processing 5.0.0. Size distribution and number concentration of the microbubble precursors were characterized via Coulter counter measurements (Multisizer 4e, Beckman Coulter, Inc., Brea, CA, USA) using a 20 µm aperture tube. For the measurements, a sample of 50 µL was added to 100 mL filtered Isoton II diluent and continuously stirred at 5 rpm. ## **2.3. Experimental setup** The photon radiation response of the different nanodroplet formulations was evaluated using a Small Animal Radiation Research Platform (SARRP) from Xstrahl Ltd. (Walsall Wood, United Kingdom), featuring a 225 kV X-ray tube. Nanodroplets were homogenously dispersed in 100 mL deionized water in custom, 3D-printed phantom containers (6 x 5 cm², figure 1). The latter contained imaging fiducials (purple arrows in figure 1b) visible in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) to facilitate a reproducible positioning of the isocenter. A single, 10 x 10 mm² radiation field was applied using a brass collimator and placed within the left half of the phantom container as seen in the yellow pane (bottom right) in figure 1b. This way, the right half of the phantom served as an internal control, albeit still subject to stray radiation. A thermocouple was placed inside the phantom container to monitor the temperature and to provide feedback to control an integrated heating element maintaining the temperature during long (2 Gy) irradiations. **==> picture [455 x 235] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 1.** Experimental set-up of the phantom irradiation experiments. (a) Photograph of the experimental set-up indicating its most important elements: (1) photon beam shaped to a 10 x 10 mm² radiation field using a brass collimator; (2) 3D-printed phantom container containing freely floating nanodroplet samples in deionized water; (3) ultrasound probe in a probe holder connected to the phantom container for reproducible ultrasound imaging during irradiation; (4) temperature control unit consisting of a thermocouple placed in the water in the phantom, a temperature display and a heating element to maintain the temperature during the long (2 Gy) irradiations. (b) CBCT scan of the water-filled phantom container acquired by the SARRP system and used to design the radiation treatment plan. Purple and green arrows indicate imaging fiducials added to the phantom container to reproducibly position the isocenter (yellow star). The yellow pane (bottom right) aligns with the plane of ultrasound imaging and the red box represents the 10 x 10 mm² radiation field. ## **2.4. Ultrasound imaging** A 7.5 MHz L7-XTech probe (Vermon, Tours, France) was positioned onto the phantom container using a probe holder for online ultrasound imaging during irradiation. The probe was connected to an ULA-OP 256 research platform (X-Phase srl, Florence, Italy), which was located just outside of the shielded SARRP system. Two different imaging sequences were used depending on the frame rate and scan duration. For long acquisitions, all 128 transducer elements of the probe were used to transmit plane waves (15 angles compounding from -7.5 to +7.5 degrees), with a pulse repetition frequency of 400 Hz, resulting in a frame rate of 27 Hz. Given the available buffer size, this allowed for a total acquisition time of ~100 s, able to capture the full delivery of a 2 Gy fraction (~72 s). For high-frame rate imaging, a pulse repetition frequency of 6 kHz resulted in a frame rate of 400 Hz, able to capture the fast response dynamics at the onset of irradiation in a ~7 s acquisition window. Again, 15 plane waves were compounded as before. Depending on the nanodroplet core and operation temperature, different (low) transmit acoustic pressures were used to ensure no vaporization events were triggered acoustically. ## **2.5. In phantom photon radiation response** The radiation conditions for the different phantom experiments are listed in table 1. The response of pure OFP droplets was evaluated at increasing temperatures: 21 °C, 28 °C and 33 °C. For the mixed-core droplets, all irradiations were performed at 37 °C. Most irradiations were imaged using the high-frame rate sequence. Given the limited buffer size, radiation dose was set to 0.1 Gy, which corresponded to an irradiation of ~4 s at the maximally achievable dose rate of 1.67 Gy/min. A dose of 2 Gy was applied for the low-frame rate acquisition. Finally, two negative control experiments were conducted: the irradiation of (i) one phantom without droplets and (ii) three phantoms with pure DFB droplets, featuring a reduced degree of superheat below the expected photon sensitization limit. **Table 1.** Phantom irradiation conditions. ||**Operation**

Image processing** _et al_ Raw ultrasound signals were first beamformed using the delay-and-sum method (Perrot 2021) weighted by the coherence factor (Matrone _et al_ 2020), with subsequent coherent compounding of the 15 transmitted plane waves. Then, the obtained images were bandpass filtered (Butterworth, 2-20 MHz), envelope-detected through Hilbert transformation and eventually log-compressed to dB-scale. Finally, gray values across all images were normalized by subtraction of a fixed value (75 dB). Average gray values throughout the acquisition were determined in a 10 x 10 mm² region-of-interest (ROI) delimiting the radiation field and positioned using the imaging fiducial visible both in CBCT and ultrasound images (green arrow in figure 1b). As saving of the ultrasound data was triggered manually, small variations in the onset of the radiation response during the ultrasound acquisition were expected. Therefore, the start of irradiation was determined from the average gray value in the ROI as follows. For high frame rate acquisitions, first a 100 ms moving average was applied to the quantified response. Then, the first derivative was calculated, which was subsequently filtered by a 100 ms (40 frames) moving average. The frame of radiation onset was then defined as the first of hundred consecutive frames with a positive slope exceeding an empirical threshold. For low frame rate acquisitions, the same approach was followed, but the moving average filter was changed to 111 ms (3 frames) and the onset frame was the first of 27 consecutive frames with a positive slope exceeding the threshold. In cases where this approach failed due to a low radiation response, either the complete ultrasound acquisition is shown or the start of irradiation was set to the theoretical start (after 3 s of the 7 s acquisition). For visualization purposes, displayed quantifications were cropped from 1 s before the presumed irradiation onset to the end of the irradiation. ## **3. Results** ## **3.1 The degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core strongly influences the photon response** To illustrate the importance of the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core, we first irradiated pure OFP droplets at different temperatures covering the complete photon-sensitive zone: 21 °C (s = 0.53), 28 °C (s = 0.60) and 33 °C (s = 0.64). The photon response and its dynamics are displayed in figure 2. **==> picture [455 x 270] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 2.** Photon radiation response of pure OFP nanodroplets at different degrees of superheat. B-mode images at different time points with respect to the start of the irradiation: -0.5 s (a, e, i), +0.5 s (b, f, j) and +2 s (c, g, k), shown for a representative phantom at each temperature: 21 °C (a-c), 28 °C (e-g) and 33 °C (i-k). The phantoms were irradiated with a dose of 0.1 Gy at a dose rate of 1.67 Gy/min. The red box indicates the 10 x 10 mm² radiation field and quantification ROI. The final column (d, h, l) shows the corresponding dynamics of the quantification of the average gray value for the entire ultrasound acquisition for three different phantoms (prepared from the same vial). The red curve corresponds to the displayed B-mode images. Vertical dashed lines correspond to the different time points of the B-mode images (irradiation starts at ~1 s). At 21 °C, just above the photon sensitization threshold, we notice that the radiation response is small with a near linear increase of the average gray value after irradiation started (figure 2d). Note the large amount of background bubbles. As these were already present before irradiation started, they are attributed to suboptimal nanodroplet synthesis (relying on microbubble condensation). Indeed, a repeat of the radiation experiment at 21 °C with a new nanodroplet vial barely showed any background signals (figure S1). At 28 °C, a much stronger radiation response was observed with barely any background bubbles prior to irradiation. Initially, gray value increase is near linear, but rapidly slows down towards a plateau. Finally, at 33 °C, the radiation-induced ultrasound contrast follows a clear sigmoid curve, with a fast rise time. As droplets and radiation-induced microbubbles were free-floating, the microbubble cloud flows out of the radiation field over time. Sparse vaporizations appear beyond the red radiation field as a result of stray radiation. We also attempted to irradiate the pure OFP nanodroplets at 37 °C (s = 0.68). However, a high degree of spontaneous vaporization at this elevated degree of superheat prevented an ultrasound read-out. Despite variability in the background levels as reflected in the gray value level before irradiation starts, the dynamics of the contrast generation were highly reproducible for different phantoms prepared from the same nanodroplet vial, indicating high intra-vial reproducibility. Finally, to confirm ultrasound contrast was solely induced by radiation-induced droplet vaporization, we also irradiated a water phantom without droplets at 37 °C. As expected, no microbubbles were formed and hence no radiation-induced ultrasound contrast was generated (figure S2). ## **3.2 DFB nanodroplets are insufficiently superheated to generate a photon response at body temperature** To overcome the poor stability of OFP nanodroplets at body temperature, higher boiling point liquid cores can be used. For instance, we repeated the previous radiation experiments at 37°C with pure DFB droplets (figure 3). Due to the boiling point of -2 °C, DFB droplets feature a reduced superheat of only s = 0.34 at 37 °C. This explains the lack of radiation response observed in all of the irradiated phantoms. **==> picture [455 x 96] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 3.** Photon radiation response of pure DFB nanodroplets at 37 °C. B-mode images at different time points during ultrasound acquisition (1 s, 3.5 s, 6 s) are shown for a representative phantom (a-c). The phantom was irradiated with a dose of 0.1 Gy at a dose rate of 1.67 Gy/min. The irradiation starts at ~3 s. The red box indicates the 10 x 10 mm² radiation field and quantification ROI. The final column (d) shows the corresponding dynamics of the quantification of the average gray value for the entire ultrasound acquisition for three different phantoms (prepared from the same vial). The red curve corresponds to the displayed B- mode images. Vertical dashed lines correspond to the different time points of the B-mode images. Note that for the black curve in panel (d), we only reached 35.5 °C during irradiation. These observations highlight that pure liquid cores lack the flexibility to tune the nanodroplet degree of superheat to exhibit a strong photon response, while maintaining good stability at body temperature. ## **3.3 Mixed-core nanodroplets allow to tune the degree of superheat to generate a strong radiation response at body temperature** To overcome the limitations of pure PFC cores, we propose to mix different perfluorocarbons to obtain a photon-sensitive nanodroplet formulation at body temperature. Theoretical calculations using Raoult’s law estimate that for a 17:4 volumetric ratio of OFP:DFB the reduced degree of superheat is s ≈ 0.63, assuming an ideal mixture behavior. Figure 4 shows the photon response of these mixed-core nanodroplets after irradiation at 37 °C for 12 different irradiations, spread over four different nanodroplet vials. A video of the radiation response can be found in the supplementary materials (video S1). **==> picture [455 x 372] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 4.** Photon radiation response of 17:4 OFP:DFB nanodroplets at 37 °C. B-mode images at different time points with respect to the start of the irradiation: -0.5 s (a, e, i, m), +0.5 s (b, f, j, n) and +2 s (c, g, k, o), shown for a representative phantom of four different nanodroplet vials (a-c, e-g, i-k and m-o). The phantoms were irradiated with a dose of 0.1 Gy at a dose rate of 1.67 Gy/min. The red box indicates the 10 x 10 mm² radiation field and the quantification ROI. The final column (d, h, l and p) shows the corresponding dynamics of the quantification of the average gray value over time for three different phantoms (prepared from the same vial). The red curve corresponds to the displayed B-mode images. Vertical dashed lines correspond to the different time points of the B-mode images. A clear radiation response was observed in each case, primarily confined to the radiation field, and with very limited background bubbles present prior to irradiation. Looking at the dynamics of the contrast generation, good reproducibility was observed for phantoms prepared from the same nanodroplet vial. However, a non-negligible variation in both the overall radiation response and the response dynamics was observed for phantoms prepared from different nanodroplet vials, indicating substantial inter-vial variability. For example, while the background signals for all phantoms hovered around -80 dB, the peak signals (plateaus) varied between circa -65 to -50 dB. The variability of the radiation response is also clear from comparing the B-mode images at the final time point. Where in some phantoms the microbubble cloud fills the entire ROI (figure 4c,o), in certain phantoms large empty zones remain (figure 4g,k). ## **3.4 The manual nanodroplet synthesis and different fugacity of the mixed-core liquids result in substantial variability in the radiation response** Two hypotheses could explain the observed inter-vial variability for mixed-core droplets. First, as the photon response strongly relies on the exact degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core, it also strongly depends on its exact composition. To evaluate whether both perfluorocarbons were indeed incorporated in a 17:4 ratio as expected from the synthesis protocol,[19] F NMR spectroscopy was performed (figure 5). While both perfluorocarbons were incorporated in the nanodroplet core, substantial differences in their relative proportion existed between different nanodroplet vials. Moreover, a rapid decrease in OFP:DFB ratio was observed over time, which can further alter the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core. The impact of the latter on our radiation experiments was minimized by keeping the vials on ice and using the nanodroplet vials immediately after preparation (within ~15 min). The rapid diffusion of OFP out of the droplet core (explaining lower OFP:DFB ratios at later time points), in combination with the 30 min time window between the end of droplet preparation and the end of the first NMR measurement, also explains why even at t = 0 h, the molar ratio 5.3:1 expected from the 17:4 volumetric ratio (dashed horizontal line in figure 5c), is not reached. The inter-vial variability in OFP:DFB ratio at the initial time point could contribute to the variability observed in the radiation response for different vials shown in figure 4. **==> picture [449 x 285] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 5.**[19] F NMR spectroscopy of 17:4 OFP:DFB mixed-core nanodroplets over time. If the variability of the photon response in mixed-core droplets is solely due to the presence of multiple liquids in the nanodroplet core, one would expect no (or much less) variability for pure core droplets. Therefore, we irradiated three phantoms containing pure OFP droplets from different nanodroplet vials at 28 °C. Given the extended duration of the irradiation, free-floating microbubbles had time to flow out of the radiation field. Hence, we only show the response dynamics for different nanodroplet vials (figure 8). A full video of the radiation response of a representative phantom is available as supplementary material (Video S2). Similarly to the short 0.1 Gy irradiations, the signal rapidly reaches a plateau value, which is relatively maintained for the entire irradiation. Different nanodroplet concentrations (200 and 50 µL) yielded different plateau values, with the higher concentration reaching higher ultrasound gray values (figure 8a). **==> picture [357 x 145] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 8.** Photon radiation response of 17:4 OFP:DFB nanodroplets at 37 °C. Vertical dashed lines indicate the start of the irradiation. Note that for the black curve with the lowest “plateau” in panel (a) we only reached 35.1 °C during irradiation. ## **4. Discussion** We evaluated different photon-sensitive nanodroplet compositions for ultrasound-based photon dosimetry at body temperature. This required a nanodroplet formulation exhibiting a strong photon response on the one hand, while maintaining sufficient stability on the other hand. ## **4.1 Importance of the nanodroplet degree of superheat on the photon radiation response** To illustrate the importance of the degree of superheat on the photon response, we first irradiated OFP droplets at different temperatures. D’Errico previously described a fluid-dependent temperature range in which superheated emulsions are photon-sensitive (between s = 0.51 and s = 0.65, D’Errico, 2001). The vertical dashed lines in figure 9a delimit this photon-sensitive zone for pure OFP. Interestingly, when plotting the average signal increase between the start and end of the irradiation, a linear relationship was observed with the lowest (highest) radiation response observed at the temperature closest to the lower (upper) limit of the photon-sensitive zone. As the dB scale log-compresses the data, this linear behavior is in agreement with the exponential increase in count rates observed by D’Errico with increasing temperature (D’Errico 2001). Unfortunately, the upper limit for OFP is lower than body temperature, preventing its use for in vivo applications. While this upper limit can be shifted to higher temperatures by improving droplet stability via an appropriate shell (e.g. lipid, polymer) or decreasing the nanodroplet size (additional contribution of the Laplace pressure will increase the boiling point, reducing the degree of superheat), the lipid-shelled OFP droplets used in the present study did not survive the experimental procedures to evaluate their radiation response at 37 °C. On the contrary, pure DFB droplets did not exhibit sufficient superheat to be sensitive to photons at 37 °C. **==> picture [361 x 155] intentionally omitted <==** **Figure 9.** Average gray value increase between the start and end of photon irradiation in a 10 x 10 mm² ROI covering the entire radiation field for pure OFP droplets at varying temperatures (a), and for different droplet compositions at varying degree of superheat (b). Phantoms were irradiated with 0.1 Gy at 1.67 Gy/min. Data points in panel (a) refer to the irradiations presented in figure 2 and figure 6, while in panel (b) also the data points of figure 4 are added. The solid black line shows the linear fit to the data points: (a) y = 2.0890x – 36.4517, R² = 0.8762; (b) y = 222.9x – 111.3, R² = 0.5739, while the vertical dashed lines delimit the theoretical photon-sensitive zone of superheated emulsions. D’Errico also described that the radiation response of different emulsions can be directly compared when the absolute temperatures are converted to the reduced degree of superheat (𝑠, equation 1) (D’Errico 2001). In that case, one would expect the radiation response of mixed-core droplets to follow the same trend. While true on average (figure 9b), the large inter-vial variability, reflected in the large drop in R² value (0.88 to 0.57) of the trendline fit when adding the mixed-core data points, prevents to make conclusive claims. Note that evaluating the radiation response based on the gray value increase is not optimal as the gray values are influenced by saturation of the ultrasound signal, attenuation by the existing microbubble cloud and nanodroplet depletion effects. Nevertheless, figure 9 confirms the importance of the degree of superheat of the nanodroplet core to tune the photon response. ## **4.2 Importance of the nanodroplet formulation on the photon radiation response** Based on theoretical considerations, we opted for a 17:4 OFP:DFB nanodroplet formulation corresponding to a reduced degree of superheat s ≈ 0.63. This formulation yielded a strong photon response with minimal background bubbles due to spontaneous vaporization. Nevertheless, the strong fugacity (= tendency to escape the core (Brambila _et al_ 2020)) of OFP in combination with the thin lipid shell and manual synthesis method, resulted in a short shelf-life with strong fluctuations in the nanodroplet core composition and overall yield. These fluctuations manifested themselves in substantial inter-vial variability, which has to be overcome to enable quantitative dose read-outs. Lipid-shelled nanodroplets (and microbubbles) are notorious for their poor shelf-life. Sometimes thicker, polymeric shells are preferred (Hadinoto _et al_ 2013, Sirsi and Borden 2009). While they reduce diffusion out of the core, they are unfortunately not compatible with the microbubble condensation method. Indeed, lipid shells can reorganize by shedding excess lipids upon volume compression. Instead, rigid polymeric shells tend to break, generating local openings through which the core rapidly escapes (Bloch _et al_ 2004). Hence, to prepare polymeric nanodroplets, the core material needs to be liquid from the start of the synthesis. This raises challenges for the used low-boiling point liquids. While OFP (boiling point = -37 °C) can be easily liquified e.g. by placing a glass vial in liquid nitrogen, the aqueous lipid solution would instantly freeze, preventing droplet formation. Similarly, microfluidic approaches have been proposed to improve the reproducibility of the nanodroplet production (Martz _et al_ 2012, Melich _et al_ 2020), but they feature the same challenges for low-boiling point liquids. In addition, they suffer from low production yields. An alternative synthesis process called the ouzo method, relies on saturating a co-solvent with _et al_ perfluorocarbons before adding a poor solvent with dissolved lipidic shell precursors (Li 2019). This forces droplet nucleation, even for gaseous low-boiling point perfluorocarbons. Yet, the monolayer lipid shell still limits long-term droplet stability. While some flexibility exists in modifying the lipid composition to modulate shell permeability (Garg _et al_ 2013), more promising is the transition towards hybrid lipid-polymer shells (Hadinoto _et al_ 2013). Recently, Wang and colleagues showed that adding pluronic F-68 to a lipid microbubble shell strongly enhances the microbubble stability by preventing coalescence (Wang _et al_ 2025). As part of our future work, we aim to explore whether such enhanced microbubble stability also translates to an improved nanodroplet shelf-life. If an equally responsive, but more stable nanodroplet formulation can be found, most of the limitations discussed above are easily solved. Firstly, reduction of diffusion out of the nanodroplet core would prevent rapidly fluctuating core ratios in mixed-core droplets, ensuring a more stable radiation response. Secondly, if shelf-life is improved, nanodroplet concentrations can be determined prior to irradiation (e.g. via nanoparticle tracking analysis), to account for residual differences in nanodroplet yield, further reducing inter-vial variability. Thirdly, a centrifugal size selection step could be added to the protocol after microbubble condensation to yield a more monodisperse nanodroplet population (Collado-Lara _et al_ 2023), again minimizing the variability of the radiation response. In this paper, we only explored a single mixture of perfluorocarbons. Other mixtures might exhibit a more optimal radiation response. While optimizing the mixture is important, this is best performed when testing the droplets in an in vivo context. Intravenous injection, blood pressure fluctuations, (bio)chemical interactions, etc. may all influence the nanodroplet stability in vivo. Depending on the exact requirements these factors impose on the droplet stability and thus the upper limit of superheat that can be used in an in vivo setting, the droplet composition can be further improved. ## **4.3 Limitations and future perspectives** To minimally influence the photon response, we opted for freely floating nanodroplets, which were not stirred during irradiation. This caused the generated microbubbles to flow out of the irradiated zone over time as particularly noticeable for the long irradiations (video S2). This also limited the replenishment of nanodroplets to passive diffusion. Remarkably, signal plateaus were largely maintained for the entire 2 Gy irradiation, indicating that the outflow of microbubbles was balanced by the vaporization of fresh nanodroplets. Moreover, different plateau levels were reached for different nanodroplet concentrations, indicating the possibility to modulate the radiation-induced ultrasound response by varying the nanodroplet concentration. This is in agreement with earlier findings that the radiation response is dependent on the nanodroplet concentration (volume fraction) and the effective fluence of particles contributing to vaporization events (in this case photon-induced electrons) (Collado-Lara _et al_ 2023, Carlier _et al_ 2026). In vivo, we envision to detect vaporization events directly in circulation. Depending on the circulatory lifetime of the droplets, we expect to continuously replenish the nanodroplet supply and wash out generated microbubbles, preventing rapid saturation of the ultrasound signals. Noteworthy, in vivo, nanodroplets would be confined by vessels, potentially influencing their vaporization response as previously observed for acoustic droplet vaporization (Lin _et al_ 2017). While the radiation stimulus will be less affected by attenuation than an ultrasound trigger, the limited room for expansion may reduce the number of observed vaporization events. Quantification of the (dynamics of) the radiation-induced ultrasound contrast relied on the evaluation of gray values extracted from conventional B-mode sequences. While sufficient for simple phantom setups with minimal background, more adequate contrast sequences will be required in vivo. For this purpose, we are currently implementing dedicated amplitude modulation (AM) and amplitude-modulated pulse inversion (AMPI) sequences, which are particularly sensitive to the non-linear oscillations of generated microbubbles and “mute” tissue background (Mine _et al_ 2024). In addition, we are developing an ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) pipeline (Errico _et al_ 2015, Collado-Lara _et al_ 2022, Heymans _et al_ 2025). Benefitting from highframe rate acquisitions or passive detection, we should be able to localize individual vaporization events with µm-level precision. By tracking bubbles over subsequent frames, one can (partially) discriminate between newly generated bubbles and bubbles flowing around. However, using 2D ultrasound imaging, it remains difficult to distinguish between droplets flowing through the elevational plane and those that are newly vaporized. To overcome this problem, we are setting up a matrix probe eventually enabling to capture vaporization events and track generated microbubbles in 3D. Reliable vaporization counts would enable to establish truly quantitative dose-response relationships, if the nanodroplet concentration and radiation dose in the blood stream are known. The former can be determined by evaluating the circulatory lifetime of the contrast agent and by choosing the appropriate injection approach (bolus vs continuous infusion), while the latter would be simulated using the HEDOS framework (Shin _et al_ 2021). ## **5. Conclusion** For the first time, we demonstrated strong photon-induced ultrasound contrast using mixed-core nanodroplets, paving the way for future in vivo dosimetry applications. We illustrated the importance of the degree of superheat, with nanodroplets exhibiting a photon response only within a relatively small thermal range. A trade-off exists between a stronger photon response (higher degree of superheat) and the stability of the droplet formulation. In this regard, pure perfluorocarbon cores offer insufficient flexibility to modulate the response at body temperature as illustrated for octafluoropropane (OFP, spontaneous vaporization) and decafluorobutane (DFB, no photon response) cores. Mixed-core droplets allowed to tune the degree of superheat to ensure a strong radiation response at body temperature, as demonstrated for a 17:4 OFP:DFB core for photon doses as small as 0.1 Gy. The use of perfluorocarbons with different fugacity and the employed synthesis approach resulted in substantial variability in the nanodroplet yield and composition. Core composition also rapidly changed over time due to the preferential diffusion of the more volatile (OFP) compound. These factors manifested themselves in non-negligible inter-vial variability of the radiation response. Alternative nanodroplet formulations with an improved stabilizing shell will be required to strengthen reproducibility. In combination with the transition from semi-quantitative gray value read-outs to the detection of individual vaporization events, this may eventually enable quantitative dosimetric read-outs. ## **6. paper.title: Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pre-training
paper.abstract: Medical Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) leverages the semantic richness of radiology reports to learn 3D representations, yet current architectures remain fundamentally anatomy-agnostic. While clinical diagnostics rely on organ-specific context, standard encoders apply a uniform, dense parameterization to all volumetric patches, and existing Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routers gate on isolated local features without explicit access to the organ composition of the scan or crop. We propose Anatomy-Activated Mixture-of-Experts (A$^{2}$MoE), a framework that incorporates anatomical inductive biases within the model's computational path. A$^{2}$MoE introduces two key components: (1) a Histogram Representation Router (HRR) that conditions expert selection on global visual context and a predicted anatomical composition histogram, encouraging anatomy-dependent expert weighting; and (2) an Organ-Query Multi-Scale Projector (OQMSP) that utilizes learnable queries to extract organ-level embeddings for fine-grained alignment without requiring manual annotations at inference. By routing at the patch level rather than the token level, A$^{2}$MoE reduces routing complexity by orders of magnitude while satisfying load balancing by construction. Pre-trained on over 60,000 multi-phase CT scans, A$^{2}$MoE achieves state-of-the-art performance across segmentation, classification, and detection benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our anatomically grounded inductive biases support robust generalization to MRI and ultrasound, establishing a scalable foundation for medical representation learning. The code is available at https://github.com/gmum/A2MoE.

paper.title: Integrating Deep PPG Representations and Digital Biomarkers for Aortic Stenosis Detection with Peri-TAVI Assessment
paper.abstract: Access to echocardiography is often limited, delaying recognition of progressive aortic stenosis (AS). A brief, low-cost physiological measurement obtained during routine care could help identify patients who may warrant earlier imaging. Here, we present PulseAS, integrating deep photoplethysmography (PPG) representations, waveform biomarkers and clinical information for high-grade AS screening. Three complementary analyses assessed (1) validation and transfer across cohorts differing in geography and ethnic composition, (2) score-based enrichment of AS and pre-transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) cases, and (3) preoperative and postoperative pulse changes. Using 15-s recordings, separate patient-level cross-validation in EDU (n = 1,209) and MIMIC-III (n = 2,970) yielded AUROCs of 0.818 (PulseAS-XGB) and 0.838 (PulseAS-L2), respectively. In external validation from MIMIC-III to EDU, PulseAS-XGB achieved an AUROC of 0.716, improving to 0.813 after local adaptation. The highest-scoring 10% captured 45.2% of all high-grade AS cases in EDU and 41.3% in MIMIC-III, and 56.9% of pre-TAVI cases in EDU. Notably, in the EDU TAVI subgroup, PPG waveforms showed earlier systolic peaks and narrower systolic contours following intervention. These findings support clinical-PPG risk stratification in new populations and warrant prospective evaluation of echocardiographic prioritisation.

paper.title: Energy-Efficient Tri-Hybrid Beamforming with Movable Pattern-Reconfigurable Antennas
paper.abstract: Conventional hybrid precoding is confined to the digital/analog domains, leaving the spatial and radiation-pattern degrees-of-freedoms (DoFs) largely untapped. To unlock these, we propose a movable pattern-reconfigurable antenna (MPRA) and an energy-efficient tri-hybrid framework that jointly optimizes the precoders, antenna positions, and radiation-pattern states. We develop a hardware-inspired power model capturing the energy and transmission-time costs of antenna reconfiguration. The resulting mixed discrete-continuous fractional problem is solved via an alternating-optimization framework combining fractional programming, Riemannian optimization, and switching-aware pattern optimization. Simulations demonstrate near-exhaustive-search performance and consistent energy-efficiency (EE) gains, validating the complementary benefits of antenna movement, pattern reconfiguration, and tri-hybrid precoding under hardware-inspired power and latency costs.

\section{Introduction}
\subsection{Background and Literature Reviews}
In the era of sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications, the scarcity of spectrum resources and the explosive growth in heterogeneous service demands have driven researchers to explore more efficient and flexible transmission technologies \cite{1}. To further enhance spectral and interference management in dense wireless deployments, rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) has recently emerged as a highly promising transmission strategy \cite{2}. By splitting messages into common and private components and superimposing them through linear precoding, RSMA provides flexible interference handling. Owing to this flexibility, RSMA demonstrates improved robustness against imperfect channel state information and offers superior rate-reliability trade-offs in interference-limited environments \cite{3}. However, despite its advantages, the performance of RSMA may still be insufficient in highly dynamic or heavily loaded networks, where interference suppression remains challenging. To further maximize its performance potential, successive interference cancellation (SIC) from non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) \cite{noma} can be incorporated into RSMA, forming a hybrid structure. By combining rate-splitting capability of RSMA with power-domain multiplexing of NOMA \cite{7}, such hybrid design enhances multi-user signal separation and strengthens interference mitigation, enabling greater spectral efficiency and improved link reliability. However, the performance of such multiple accesses is often hindered by severe channel fading and inter-user interference, which potentially degrades the signal quality and limits its practical deployment \cite{9}. 
To address the above-mentioned issues, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have been proposed as an enabling technology \cite{10, 11}. By adjusting the configuration of RIS elements, a virtual line-of-sight (LoS) link can be established to bypass obstacles between the transmitter and receiver and to improve the signal quality for combating the channel fading \cite{my_fdris3, 12}. Benefited from these advantages, RIS can enable precise signal distribution, significantly improving communication performances. Although RIS holds promise for next-generation wireless networks, its practical deployment remains constrained by several inherent limitations. Specifically, it can only be operated over a 180-degree half-space coverage area, and mainly depends on external power supplies, which confines its independent operation and scalability. To overcome the backdrops, the concept of multi-functional RIS (MF-RIS) has been introduced in \cite{14, my_ojcom}, integrating simultaneous transmission and reflection (STAR) capabilities to provide 360-degree full-space coverage and ubiquitous connectivity \cite{15, 16, my_star}. Additionally, MF-RIS is equipped with radio-frequency (RF) and energy harvesting (EH) circuits, enabling it to capture energy from incident electromagnetic signals and is capable of operating in a self-sustainable manner \cite{18, 19, 20}. Such design alleviates the dependence on wired power infrastructure or frequent battery replacement, enhancing the overall energy efficiency (EE). Furthermore, by embedding active components, MF-RIS is capable of conducting signal amplification \cite{22} for compensating severe path loss, improving the quality-of-services (QoS) of users in weak channel conditions. When combined with advanced multiple access schemes, MF-RIS can substantially strengthen the propagation conditions for user clusters, especially under NOMA-/RSMA-based transmissions. 
However, the practical implementation of active MF-RIS is also hindered by hardware-induced constraints such as the coupled phase-shift effects \cite{23}. Unlike ideal models, active components frequently exhibit a strong interdependence between the phase-shift and amplification gains \cite{24}. This coupling effect might reduce the available DoFs in the optimization space, which necessitates more complex coordination strategies to achieve the desired beamforming gains. To overcome these limitations, beyond static metasurfaces, fluid antenna (FA) systems have recently attracted attention for their ability to dynamically reconfigure the effective antenna position within a given aperture by leveraging fluid-based elements \cite{my_lim, 26}. Similar to FA, movable-antenna (MA) structures \cite{MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4} are also developed. By allowing the radiating point to move within a predefined region, FA/MA can exploit spatial diversity in small-scale fading without requiring multiple RF chains, offering new degrees of freedom (DoFs) at the physical layer. This dynamic ability is particularly appealing in environments with rapidly varying channels or strong blockage effects. In the works of \cite{new1, new2}, antenna position of the MA is deployed to increase the spatial DoF and enhance the performance of the integrated sensing and communication systems. The paper \cite{new3} investigates that the MA is capable of achieving full array gain over the desired direction, whereas null steering in undesired directions can be realized. The work of \cite{new4} further discusses near-field digital and analog beamforming in MA-aided multiuser communication systems. In the work of \cite{6dma}, six-dimensional MA is introduced that exploits the transceiver spatial variation by considering both xyz-positions and rotations to improve performance in terms of geometric array gains, spatial multiplexing and interference mitigation. Inspired by the FA/MA \cite{fas1, 10, MA1, new1, new2, new3, new4}, the movable-elements (ME) are introduced \cite{25, lim1, pat, movele1} to enable element-wise spatial adjustment across three-dimensional (3D) Cartesian axes of xyz-domain. Different from MAs, ME-enhanced RIS further aligning to proper small-scale channels induces a more challenging task when configuring well-positioned elements in the cascaded channels from the base station (BS), RIS to users \cite{lim1}. The authors in \cite{26} have proposed a movable-element RIS (ME-RIS) framework, utilizing an element-wise position optimization approach to significantly enhance beamforming gains. Furthermore, the concept of fluid-element STAR surfaces called FIRES is designed in \cite{27}, which extends the FA capability to STAR-RIS architectures. In paper \cite{new5}, MA-aided NOMA is considered for multi-user downlink communications, where the MA positions at the users, BS beamforming, and SIC decoding indicators are jointly optimized. Moreover, the work of \cite{new6} investigates the benefits of FA with dynamic port reconfiguration for enhancing RSMA performance, where the outage probability and ergodic rate are analyzed to quantify the performance gains provided by FA. However, most existing FA/MA-integrated works focus on single-link scenarios or basic reflection/transmission structures, relying on the external power grid usage. The integration of ME into MF-RISs that simultaneously supports element mobility, reflection/transmission capability, signal amplification, and self-sustainable EH remains largely unexplored. 
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), the integration of learning-based optimizations into wireless communication systems has become an important research trend \cite{11, 29}, especially for complex environments. Owing to the strong coupling between multiple strategies such as beamforming and RIS configurations, the resulting optimization problems typically exhibit high dimensionality, non-linearity, and mixed discrete-continuous structures, rendering traditional analytical or convex-approximation methods inadequate in highly dynamic environments. In addressing these challenges, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has been widely adopted for resource allocation and control \cite{11, my_rl_wu, 30, han, 31, my_rl_yt} thanks to its capability of learning near-optimal policies from interactions with complex environments. In DRL, an agent performs the determined actions and then attains rewards, followed by the observed updated states for the next-round policy decision. In \cite{11}, a multi-agent system is considered, where each agent corresponds to an individual RIS, and the joint beamforming and RIS deployment are optimized using multi-agent RL techniques. In paper \cite{29}, a multi-agent system is designed for low-complexity beamforming and power control in multi-antenna-based NOMA networks. The work of \cite{my_rl_wu} designs a hierarchical RL structure for RIS optimizations, where the core-RL optimizes the beamforming and configurations, whereas auxiliary RL optimizes the hyperparameters of core-RL for better learning process. Nonetheless, most existing DRL approaches are either centralized, leading to scalability and overhead issues, or designed for purely continuous or purely discrete state-action spaces, which are inadequate for complex wireless networks. This motivates the development of hybrid DRL frameworks that can handle continuous-discrete action spaces in a unified manner \cite{30, han, 31, my_ojcom}. In the work of \cite{30}, hybrid continuous and discrete action outputs are designed as a parametrized sharing architecture. Extended from \cite{30}, the paper \cite{han} designs hybrid DRL for tackling continuous STAR-RIS configurations and the discrete coupled-phase problems. The work of \cite{31} designs twin-models and bi-directional sharing structure in hybrid DRL architecture for complex MF-RIS policies associated with continuous-discrete actions. 
Furthermore, conventional DRL architectures relying solely on multiple deep neural layer learning may struggle to capture complex dependencies between high-dimensional states and actions, especially in multi-agent coordination. To address this, adoption of transformer architectures \cite{32, my_ojcom} for enhancing feature extraction and representation learning is needed \cite{my_ojcom, 33}. Additionally, federated learning (FL) \cite{34} is utilized for enabling decentralized model aggregation and privacy-aware knowledge sharing across distributed learning agents without raw data exchange. In addition to architectural enhancements, ensuring strict adherence to operational boundaries such as QoS and power limits is crucial for practical reliability. While conventional reward shaping is often used to penalize constraint violations, its static nature frequently fails to maintain an optimal balance between performance optimization and safety requirements \cite{35, 37}. This necessitates the adoption of Lagrangian-based primal-dual optimization techniques \cite{35}, i.e., an adaptive Lagrangian multiplier method to dynamically tune penalty coefficients based on instantaneous violations. However, the applications of enhanced architectures of multi-agent hybrid DRL with transformer, parametrized sharing, federated cooperation, and adaptive Lagrangian constraint management to complex wireless network systems remain substantially unexplored. \subsection{Challenges and Contributions}
The integration of ME and MF-RIS with hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions remains unstudied but introduces several fundamental challenges. The incorporation of MEs into MF-RIS significantly enlarges the spatial DoFs, leading to a high-dimensional and highly-coupled optimization problem involving beamforming, power control, rate allocation, phase-shift coefficients, and metasurface locations as well as element positions. The comparable overhead associated with ME, including movement power consumption and repositioning delay may be introduced and cannot be neglected compared to the operational power and channel coherence time. This results in a non-convex mixed continuous-discrete problem that is difficult to solve using conventional optimization techniques. Additionally, the hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmission scheme introduces complex interference structures across clustered users, which require dynamic and coordinated resource allocation to strike a compelling balance between spectral efficiency and interference mitigation. The coupling transmissions among communication variables further increases the difficulty of joint optimization. Furthermore, the presence of EH and amplification functionalities imposes stringent system constraints of power budgets, QoS requirements, and hardware limitations. Self-sustainable capability should be achieved while supporting multiple functionalities of MF-RIS. From algorithmic perspectives, the large-scale multi-agent nature of complex wireless networks leads to scalability and non-stationarity issues, where centralized learning becomes impractical due to excessive overhead, whilst decentralized learning suffers from limited coordination and potential convergence issues. This motivates us to conceive an advanced DRL-based framework for the integration of ME and MF-RIS in hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions. The main contributions of this paper are elaborated as follows:
\begin{itemize}
	\item We propose a novel ME-enhanced MF-RIS (MM-RIS)-assisted communication framework for hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmissions. The proposed MM-RIS integrates MEs with a deployable MF-RIS capabilities, enabling adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and EH, which significantly enhances system adaptability, coverage, and energy self-sustainability in dynamic wireless environments.
	\item We formulate an EE maximization problem for the proposed MM-RIS-assisted hybrid RSMA-NOMA. The problem jointly optimizes transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS parameters of amplitude coefficients, phase-shifts, and EH ratios, as well as metasurface deployment and ME positions. The formulated problem is highly non-convex and involves mixed continuous-discrete variables with intricate coupling constraints under practical limitations such as BS power budgets, user rate requirements and rate allocation bounds as well as minimum inter-element spacing, coupled phase-shifts, self-sustainability, and deployment boundaries of MM-RIS.
	\item We develop a constrained hybrid reinforcement learning framework with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS) scheme which integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-network (MADQN) to handle continuous and discrete decision variables, respectively. A transformer-based architecture is incorporated to capture complex state-action dependencies, while FL is employed to facilitate decentralized training and accelerate convergence via collaborative knowledge sharing. Moreover, a bi-directional parametrized sharing mechanism is proposed to enable coordinated optimization across heterogeneous action spaces. Furthermore, to guarantee constraint satisfaction, a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism is conceived to dynamically update multipliers, ensuring stable and reliable learning under practical system constraints.
	\item Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed CRAFTS-enabled MM-RIS framework significantly outperforms the conventional benchmarks, including standalone PPO/DQN, non-coupled learning benchmarks, and different single-functional RIS architectures without amplification or EH in the open literature. Particularly, the proposed MM-RIS-aided RSMA-NOMA achieves substantial EE gains and constraint satisfaction across diverse scenarios, validating the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed architecture for next-generation wireless networks.
\end{itemize}
This paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{sec_sys} introduces the system model of MM-RIS-aided hybrid RSMA-NOMA and the corresponding problem formulation. Section \ref{sec_alg} elaborates the proposed framework of CRAFTS. Simulation results are provided in Section \ref{sec_sim}, whereas the conclusion is drawn in Section \ref{sec_con}.

\subsection{Channel Model}
We consider the Rician fading channel model \cite{31} between the BS and the $q$-th MM-RIS as $\mathbf{H}_{q} \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N}$
\begin{align}
	\mathbf{H}_q = \sqrt{h_0 d_{q}^{-k_0}}
\left( \sqrt{\frac{\beta_0}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{\beta_0 + 1}} \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}} \right),
\label{4}
\end{align}
where $h_0$ is the pathloss at the reference distance of 1 meter, $d_{q}= \|\mathbf{w}_b-\mathbf{w}_q\| $ is the distance between BS and MM-RIS $q$, and $k_0$ is the pathloss exponent. Notation of $\beta_0$ represents the Rician factor adjusting the portion of LoS path $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}}$ and non-LoS (NLoS) component of $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$. The LoS component $ \mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} $ is expressed as \cite{26} $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}'_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q) \mathbf{a}_b^{\mathrm{H}}(\psi_b)$,
where $(\cdot)^{\mathrm{H}}$ indicates the Hermitian operation. The transmit steering vector of the BS and the receiving steering vector of the $q$-th MM-RIS associated with the $m$-th ME are respectively given by
\begingroup
\allowdisplaybreaks
\begin{align}
	[\mathbf{a}_b(\psi_b)]_n &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} (n-1) \sin(\psi_b)}, 
	[\mathbf{a}_q(\psi'_{a,q}, \psi'_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  &= e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{a,q} \cos\psi'_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi'_{e,q}\right)},
 \label{6}
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $[ \cdot ]_n$ represents the $n$-th entry of the vector. Notation of $\lambda$ indicates the wavelength, whilst $\psi_b$ denotes the angle-of-departure (AoD) from the BS towards MM-RIS. Symbols of $\psi'_{a,q}$ and $\psi'_{e,q}$ denote the azimuth and elevation angles-of-arrival (AoAs) at MM-RIS $q$, respectively. Following \eqref{4}, the channel between the $q$-th MM-RIS and user $U_{kj}$ is defined as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj} \in \mathbb{C}^{M\times 1}$, where the distance between them is denoted as $d_{q, kj} = \| \mathbf{w}_q - \mathbf{w}_{kj} \|$. The LoS channel of $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}$ can be expressed as $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{LoS}} = \mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)$,
where $\psi''_{a,q}$ and $\psi''_{e,q}$ respectively denote the azimuth and elevation AoDs from the MM-RIS towards user $U_{kj}$, and the corresponding elementwise steering vector is defined as
\begin{align}
 [\mathbf{a}''_q (\psi''_{a,q}, \psi''_{e,q}, \mathcal{R}_q)]_m  = e^{j \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \left(x_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{a,q} \cos\psi''_{e,q} + y_{q,m} \sin\psi''_{e,q}\right)}.
 \label{eq:fires_user_channel}
\end{align}
As for the NLoS components related to MM-RIS-based channel, i.e., $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$ and $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}}$, Jake's model is adopted to model the ME-induced spatial correlation \cite{my_lim}, i.e., $[\mathbf{J}_{q}]_{i,j} = J_0 \left( \frac{2\pi \Delta d_{i,j}}{\lambda} \right)$, where $J_0$ is the Bessel function of the zero order and $\Delta d_{i,j}$ denotes the distances between the $i$-th and the $j$-th MM-RIS elements. The spatial correlation can be further written as $\mathbf{J}_{q}= \mathbf{U}_q \boldsymbol{\Lambda}_q \mathbf{U}_q^{\mathrm{H}}$, where $\mathbf{U}_q$ is the unitary matrix with eigenvectors and $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_q$ indicates the diagonal eigenvalue matrix. Accordingly, the expressions of the NLoS channels of $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}}$ and of $\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}}$ can be respectively derived by $\mathbf{H}_q^{\text{NLoS}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_q^{1/2} \mathbf{U}_q^{\mathrm{H}} \bar{\mathbf{H}}_q$ 
and
$\mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\text{NLoS}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}_{q,kj}^{1/2} \mathbf{U}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \bar{\mathbf{g}}_{q,kj}$
where $\bar{\mathbf{H}}_q$ and $\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{q,kj}$ represent the uncorrelated small-scale fading components, which are modeled as complex Gaussian distribution with zero mean and unit variance. The direct link from the BS to user $j$ at direction $k$ is denoted by $\mathbf{h}_{kj} \in \mathbb{C}^{N \times1 }$, associated with their distance of $d_{kj}$. While, the pertinent parameters of $\mathbf{h}_{kj}$ follow \eqref{4} but in a vector form, where the LoS component $ \mathbf{h}_{kj}^{\text{LoS}}$ is expressed as $\mathbf{h}^{\text{LoS}}_{kj} = \left[
1, e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}d_B\sin\varphi_{b}}, \ldots, e^{j\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}(N-1)d_B\sin\varphi_{b} } \right]^{\mathrm{T}}$, where $d_B$ denotes the element separation of BS. Notation of $\varphi_{b}$ represents the AoD of the BS towards user $U_{kj}$. Note that the NLoS part is defined as $\mathbf{h}^{\text{NLoS}}_{kj}$ following the Rayleigh fading. Consequently, the effective channel between the BS and user $U_{kj}$ is denoted as ${\mathbf{g}}_{kj} = \mathbf{h}_{kj}^{\mathrm{H}} + \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}} \mathbf{g}_{q,kj}^{\mathrm{H}} \mathbf{\Theta}_{q}^k \mathbf{H}_{q}$.
\subsection{Signal Model}
In the hybrid RSMA-NOMA downlink transmission, users are first partitioned into multiple groups to efficiently share the limited spectrum resources. Specifically, a channel-aware user grouping procedure is performed prior to resource optimization. Users are first classified according to whether they are located on the reflection or transmission side of the MM-RIS. Users on each side are then further partitioned into multiple groups according to their effective channel directions. For users $u$ and $v$, their channel correlation is defined as $\rho_{u,v} = \frac{ |\mathbf g_u\mathbf g_v^{\rm H}| }{ \|\mathbf g_u\|_2\|\mathbf g_v\|_2 }$. Users exhibiting high channel correlation are preferentially assigned to the same group to facilitate beamforming. In each group at direction $k$, data stream is split into common and private streams. The common stream decodes messages for all users, whereas the private stream provides individual data content to each user. Moreover, in private message, NOMA mechanism is employed to further superimpose private signals for enhancing the frequency utilizations. Therefore, the BS transmits signals containing the common stream $s_k^c$ and the private stream $s_{kj}$ for user $U_{kj}$. The signal received by user $U_{kj}$ can be given by

	\underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^c \sqrt{p_{k}^c} s_{k}^c }_{\text{Common Stream}}
	+ \underbrace{\sum_{l\in\mathcal{K} \backslash k } \mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_{l}^c \sqrt{p_{l}^c} s_{l}^c }_{\text{Common Interf.}} 
	+ \underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^p \sqrt{p_{kj}} s_{kj}}_{\text{Private Stream}} \notag 
	& + \underbrace{\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_k^p \sum_{i \in \mathcal{J}_k \setminus j} \sqrt{p_{ki}} s_{ki}}_{\text{Private Interf.}}
	+ \underbrace{\sum_{l \in \mathcal{K} \setminus k }\mathbf{g}_{kj} \mathbf{f}_{l}^p
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{J}_{l}} \sqrt{p_{li}} s_{li} }_{\text{Inter-Group Interf.}} \notag
	& + \underbrace{\sum_{q \in \mathcal{Q}} \mathbf{g}^{\mathrm{H}}_{q,kj}\mathbf{\Theta}_{q}^k \mathbf{n}_q}_{\text{MM-RIS-Induced Noise}} + \underbrace{{n}_{kj}}_{\text{Background Noise}}, 
\end{align}
\endgroup
where $\mathbf{f}_k^c$ and $\mathbf{f}_k^p$ represent the transmit beamforming vectors for common and private streams of the BS at direction 
$k$, respectively, satisfying the power constraint of $\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \left( \|\mathbf{f}_k^c\|^2  + \|\mathbf{f}_k^p\|^2 \right) \leq P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$, where $P_{\text{BS}}^{\text{max}}$ denotes the transmit power budge of the BS. Moreover, $p_{k}^c$ and $p_{kj}$ are defined as the power allocation factor of common message at direction $k$ and that of private messages for user $U_{kj}$, whereas $p_{k}^c+\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}_k} p_{kj} = 1$. Notation of $\mathbf{n}_{q} \sim \mathcal{CN}(0, \sigma_s^2 \mathbf{I}_M)$ denotes the amplification noise induced by the MM-RIS associated with its element noise power $\sigma_s^2$. Notation of $n_{kj}$ is background noise power of user $U_{kj}$, where its power is denoted as $\sigma_{u}^2$. Note that $\mathbf{f}_k^p$ is a group-level private precoder shared by all users within group $k$. Specifically, users with highly correlated effective channel directions are assigned to the same group and spatially served by $\mathbf f_k^p$, whereas their private messages are superimposed in the power domain using the user-specific power coefficients $p_{kj}$. Compared to assigning an independent precoder to every user, this group level design reduces the number of beamforming variables while retaining user differentiation through power-domain multiplexing.
